approachQuestion.prompt:
Inspection Route

An inspection route is an array route of integer station IDs in travel order. A request is an array request of station IDs that must be visited in that order, possibly with unrelated visits between them. Return true if distinct positions in route can match every request entry in order. The arrays are not sorted and may repeat IDs. Neither may be modified. An empty request always succeeds.

Constraints: n = route.length, m = request.length; 0 <= n,m <= 200000; IDs are in [0,1000000000].

Example 1: route = [4,2,4,7], request = [4,4,7] -> true.
Example 2: route = [4,2,7], request = [7,4] -> false.
Example 3: route = [5], request = [5,5] -> false.
constraints: Choose the most efficient valid approach for the entire stated input domain; accept equivalent optimal variants.

options.text: Scan route once with an index into request. Whenever the current route ID equals the next requested ID, advance the request index. Accept exactly when all request entries have been matched.
options.feedback: Choosing the earliest available match leaves at least as much remaining route as any later choice and consumes a distinct position each time.

options.text: Copy route, then perform the same ordered matching scan on the copy.
options.feedback: The scan is valid for every input, but the read-only scan has no reason to copy route.

options.text: For every requested ID, check that it occurs somewhere in route; ignore its position and reuse occurrences.
options.feedback: For route [5] and request [5,5], both membership checks pass, but two distinct visits are required.

options.text: For each requested entry, search route from its beginning and accept if every search finds a match.
options.feedback: For route [4,2,7] and request [7,4], separate searches succeed even though no ordered match exists.

feedback.reason: Consume the earliest possible match of each requested value without reusing a route position or imposing sorted order.
details: Return true immediately for an empty request. Otherwise walk through route in order, retaining the next unmatched request index. Advance that index only when a route value matches it. Return true once the request is exhausted, or false if route ends first.

Selecting the earliest available route match leaves the largest possible suffix for later requests. Each match consumes a distinct position; membership alone cannot handle order or repeated requested IDs.

“Scan route once with an index into request. Whenever the current route ID equals the next requested ID, advance the request index. Accept exactly when all request entries have been matched.”: Choosing the earliest available match leaves at least as much remaining route as any later choice and consumes a distinct position each time.
“Copy route, then perform the same ordered matching scan on the copy.”: The scan is valid for every input, but the read-only scan has no reason to copy route.

“For every requested ID, check that it occurs somewhere in route; ignore its position and reuse occurrences.”: For route [5] and request [5,5], both membership checks pass, but two distinct visits are required.

“For each requested entry, search route from its beginning and accept if every search finds a match.”: For route [4,2,7] and request [7,4], separate searches succeed even though no ordered match exists.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method revealed after question 1, choose its tight worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is route length and m is request length, independently variable; length access is constant time. No copy, recursion, hashing, or amortized operations. Use O(n+1) to include n=0.
constraints: Analyze this fixed method regardless of your answer to question 1; choose the tightest pair.

options.text: O(n + m + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(n + 1) time, O(n + m + 1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Scan route once; an unmatched request suffix need not be read.
details: The fixed method can return early, but in the worst case it examines every route entry, so time is O(n+1). It need not read all m request entries: when m>n, it can only inspect a prefix before failing. Only indices are retained.

Use a word-RAM model with constant-time indexed access and signed 64-bit arithmetic. Include all temporary buffers, input copies, and call frames; exclude supplied input and returned output. n is route length and m is request length, independently variable; length access is constant time. No copy, recursion, hashing, or amortized operations. Use O(n+1) to include n=0.
“O(n + m + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This is an upper bound but not the tightest for this fixed method when m is much larger than n; it never scans the whole unmatched request.
“O(n + 1) time, O(n + m + 1) auxiliary space”: No input-sized temporary storage is allocated.
“O((n + 1)(m + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Matching does not restart the route scan for each request entry.
